## Dubhlinn and the longphort

The Annals of Ulster record a longphort at Dublin in 841: a fortified ship base, the first winter camp rather than a hit-and-run raid. Dubh Linn, the black pool, was where the Poddle met the Liffey, roughly behind Dublin Castle now. The Irish name Áth Cliath, the ford of hurdles, belongs to a crossing a bit further upriver. Two names, two settlements, and they merge over time.

The longphort people were expelled in 902 and came back in 917. That gap is a good trick question.

## The Kilmainham-Islandbridge graves

Found in the 1840s and 1860s during railway works near Islandbridge. The largest group of Viking-age graves known outside the Norse homelands: swords, spearheads, shield bosses, oval brooches from women's graves. Most of it is in the National Museum, Collins Barracks and Kildare Street. The old excavation records were thin, and it was Elizabeth O'Brien who sorted out what came from where.

## Wood Quay

The excavations of 1974 to 1981, led by Pat Wallace for the National Museum. Over 3 acres of the medieval town, with house plots, wattle walls, a pre-Norman street line on Fishamble Street, combs, shoes, and the famous carved wooden crook. In 1978 about 20,000 people marched to save the site, led by Fr F. X. Martin. My father brought me on his shoulders; I was four and remember only the noise. Dublin Corporation built the Civic Offices on it anyway.

Pat Wallace, *Viking Age Dublin* (2016), the catalogue of house types, p. 412 for the Type 1 house plan I give to students.

## Sitric Silkbeard and Christ Church

Sihtric Silkbeard, king of Dublin around 989 to 1036. Struck the first coins minted in Ireland, about 997, copied from English silver pennies of Æthelred II. Made a pilgrimage to Rome in 1028 and founded Christ Church about 1030 with the first bishop, Dúnán. So the cathedral half the tourists queue at is a Hiberno-Norse foundation.

## Clontarf, 1014

Good Friday, 23 April 1014. Brian Boru's army against the Leinster king Máel Mórda and his Dublin allies, with Sigurd of Orkney brought in. Brian was killed in his tent. The schoolbook myth that Clontarf "drove the Vikings out of Ireland" is wrong twice over: it was largely an Irish political war, and the Dublin Norse stayed put. I spend a lesson on the 1014 myth and how it got made in the 19th century.

## The walking route, March 2024

14 March 2024 with a TY group of 26 and Ms Doyle from Geography. Route, about 2.1 km:

1. Wood Quay and the Civic Offices, read the plaque.
2. Fishamble Street, the line of the old street.
3. Christ Church, the crypt (school rate €4 each).
4. Down to the river and the Viking ship sculpture on the quay.
5. Back up to Dublin Castle and the Poddle culvert under the Chester Beatty garden.

Rain from step 3. Two lost umbrellas. Next time book the crypt for 11:00, not 12:30, the queue is long after midday.

## Things students get wrong

- Horned helmets: no.
- "Vikings" as an ethnicity: it was an activity. The Dublin population was mixed within two generations.
- Slavery: Dublin was one of the biggest slave markets in western Europe in the 10th and 11th centuries. Leave this out and you are telling a fairy tale.
